header: Complainant by Mr. Javed Khan Tanoli,
body: ABDUL FAYAZ, J:- Through the instant criminal appeal, the appellant Muhammad Afsar, has assailed the judgment dated 18.01.2025, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Haripur at Ghazi, whereby he was convicted under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred to as "PPC"), on two counts, and sentenced to death for committing the murders of Muhammad Ilyas and Mst. Robina Bibi, with a further direction to pay compensation amounting to Rs.10,00,000/- to the legal heirs of each deceased under section 544-A, Cr.P.C. He was also convicted under section 324, PPC, for causing firearm injuries to Haji Sher Afzal, Ghulam Fareed, Muhammad Hussain and Mst. Nageena Bibi and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment on each count, with fine of Rs.5,00,000/- for each injured person. Besides, he was also convicted under Section 337 F(v) PPC and was sentenced to five years simple imprisonment as Ta’zir with daman of Rs. 50,000/- to the victim Haji Sher Afzal; under Section 337 F(iii) PPC to simple imprisonment for three years as Ta’zir with payment of daman of Rs. 30,000/- to victim Ghulam Fareed; under section 337 F(iii) PPC to simple imprisonment for three years as Ta’zir with the direction to pay daman of Rs. 30,000/- to the victim Muhammad Hussain; under Section 337-D PPC to ten years imprisonment with Arsh amounting to 1/3 rd of Diyat to be paid to victim Mst. Nageena Bibi and under Section 337 F(iii) PPC to imprisonment of three years with direction for payment of daman amounting to Rs. 30,000/- to victim Mst. Nageena Bibi. All sentences of imprisonment were ordered to run concurrently, with the benefit of section 382-B, Cr.P.C.

2. The prosecution case, briefly stated, is that on 25.07.2011, a dispute arose between the children of the parties, following which Mst. Nasreen Bibi approached the family of the appellant. The matter was subsequently brought to the notice of Hafiz Nazakat Shah, who convened a Jirga in the Baithak of Muhammad Hussain to resolve the dispute amicably. The Jirga was attended by Haji Sher Afzal, Muhammad Gulzar, Ghulam Fareed, Muhammad Sharif, Abdul Razzaq and other notables of the locality. During the proceedings, an exchange of harsh words allegedly took place between the parties. Shortly thereafter, the appellant Muhammad Afsar, accompanied by Sher Azam and Ajmal, allegedly arrived at the place of occurrence armed with a Kalashnikov, pistol and danda, respectively. The appellant and his co-accused Sher Azam allegedly opened firing, resulting in firearm injuries to Muhammad Hussain, Haji Sher Afzal and Ghulam Fareed. Upon hearing the firing, Muhammad Ilyas, Mst. Robina Bibi and Mst. Nageena Bibi rushed towards the place of occurrence, where they also received firearm injuries. Muhammad Ilyas and Mst. Robina Bibi succumbed to their injuries, whereas the other injured persons survived. The occurrence was reported by complainant Muhammad Hussain to the local police while he himself was in an injured condition, whereupon FIR was registered. The investigating agency proceeded to inspect the place of occurrence, prepared the site plan, took into possession bloodstained earth, empties and other material objects, and recorded the statements of the prosecution witnesses. The appellant, however, could not be apprehended and was proceeded against as an absconder. He was ultimately arrested on 21.03.2021, whereafter investigation was completed against him and the supplementary challan was sent to the competent Court for trial.

3. Upon commencement of trial against the appellant, formal charge was framed against him, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In order to substantiate the accusation, the prosecution produced eighteen witnesses. On conclusion of the prosecution evidence, the appellant was examined under section 342, Cr.P.C., on 14.12.2024, wherein he denied the allegations and professed innocence. He neither opted to appear on oath under section 340(2), Cr.P.C., nor produced evidence in defence. Upon appraisal of the evidence and hearing the parties, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced him through the impugned judgment, as detailed above. Feeling aggrieved, the appellant has preferred instant appeal, whereas the learned trial Court has also sent the murder reference No. 1-A/2025. For the sake of brevity, the appeal as well as the murder reference are taken up together for decision.
4. We have heard the arguments advanced by learned counsel for the parties at considerable length and have undertaken an independent appraisal of the prosecution evidence.

5. The prosecution case against the appellant is mainly based on ocular account, medical evidence, documentary and circumstantial evidence, and the conduct of the appellant. The ocular account principally consists of the statements of PW-5 Mst. Nageena Bibi, PW-6 Ghulam Fareed, PW-7 Abdul Malik and PW-17 Haji Sher Afzal. Their statements assume particular importance because they describe the circumstances preceding the occurrence, the arrival of the accused persons at the spot followed by firing allegedly made by them. Out of these witneses, PW-5, PW-6 and PW-17 sustained injuries during the same incident, a circumstance which has considerable bearing upon the question of their presence at the place of occurrence.

6. PW-5 Mst. Nageena Bibi, stated that on the relevant date, at about 8:30 p.m., she heard the noise of firing from the direction of the Baithak of Muhammad Hussain. She, along with her brother Muhammad Ilyas and sister Mst. Robina Bibi, proceeded towards that place. According to her stance, the appellant Muhammad Afsar was armed with a Kalashnikov, while Sher Azam possessed a pistol and Ajmal was carrying a danda. She categorically attributed firing to the appellant and further stated that she sustained injuries on her right hand and abdominal region, while her brother and sister also received firearm injuries. She became seriously injured and was subsequently shifted for medical treatment.

7. The presence of the PW-5 at the spot is supported by her injuries and the corresponding medical record. The record does not disclose any material departure in her account regarding the identity of the appellant, the weapon attributed to him or his involvement in the firing. Though the said witness was relative of the deceased as well, but relationship alone does not disqualify a witness or render otherwise reliable evidence unworthy of belief. The governing consideration is whether the witness had an opportunity to observe the incident and whether the statement is truthful and consistent with the other evidence. In the case of “Ansar and others v. The State and others” (2023 SCMR 929), the Hon'ble Supreme Court has settled the importance of the testimony of an injured eyewitness whose injuries supported his presence at the scene and whose evidence remained consistent on material particulars. Applying that principle, we find that the injuries sustained by PW-5 constitute a substantial circumstance supporting her presence, while the attribution of the role to the appellant is further supported by the other prosecution witnesses. The cross-examination on the said witness failed to thrash out any ambiguity or contradiction in her stance.

8. Similarly, PW-6 Ghulam Fareed is another material witness who received firearm injuries during the occurrence. He stated that a dispute involving the children of the parties led to the convening of a Jirga at the Baithak of Muhammad Hussain. He was present there along with other participants when the appellant Muhammad Afsar arrived in the company of Sher Azam and Ajmal. According to him, the appellant was armed with a Kalashnikov and started firing towards the persons present, whereas Sher Azam was armed with a pistol. PW-6 stated that he sustained firearm injuries on his right hand and left leg, causing a fracture, and was subsequently undergone medical treatment. The account furnished by PW-6 is important for two distinct reasons. Firstly, he was present at the initial stage of the incident and therefore had an opportunity to observe the circumstances leading to the firing. Secondly, his own injuries provide independent assurance regarding his presence during the occurrence. His statement materially supports PW-5 concerning the identity of the appellant and the use of a firearm, although the two witnesses observed different stages of the incident. That distinction is significant because PW-6 was a participant in the Jirga, whereas PW-5 approached the place of occurrence after hearing the firing. Their evidence cannot be discredited merely because their respective accounts do not contain precisely identical details of the entire episode. The material question is whether their testimony is reconcilable on the central allegation regarding the appellant's participation in the armed assault. On that aspect, their statements substantially support each other.

9. PW-7 Abdul Malik, another participant in the Jirga, furnished corroboration regarding the circumstances preceding the occurrence. He deposed that he had gone to attend the Jirga at the Baithak of Muhammad Hussain and that the appellant subsequently arrived armed with a Kalashnikov, accompanied by Sher Azam and Ajmal. He further stated that the appellant and Sher Azam resorted to firing towards the persons present and that Muhammad Ilyas and Mst. Robina Bibi, who approached the scene upon hearing the shots, sustained firearm injuries. His testimony also explains the sequence in which the police reached the place of occurrence and the injured and deceased persons were dealt with. The evidence of PW-17, who also sustained injuries during the occurrence, was recorded during the proceedings under Section 512 Cr.P.C. as PW-8, however, during trial of the appellant, the said witness was reported to have died and the prosecution submitted application to the learned trial Court for transposition of evidence of the witnesses. The said application was allowed to the extent of injured PW Sher Afzal, vide order dated 10.12.2024 and consequently, his statement was transposed on the record of trial as PW-17. The said statement also corroborates the prosecution version.

10. Turning to the medical evidence, PW-1 Dr. Fozia Yasmeen, Woman Medical Officer, conducted the postmortem examination of Mst. Robina Bibi on 26.07.2011. She found injuries involving the left thigh, including an entry wound and associated injury, with a fracture of the left femur. In her opinion, death had occurred due to hypovolaemic shock resulting from firearm injury. She also examined the injured Mst. Nageena Bibi. The medical documents exhibited by her include the postmortem report and the injury report, which substantiate the occurrence of firing resulting in the death of one victim and injuries to another.

11. PW-2 Dr. Muhammad Ayaz, retired Medical Officer, conducted the postmortem examination of Muhammad Ilyas. The postmortem findings revealed multiple entry and exit wounds over different parts of his body, including the back, chest and abdominal region, accompanied by extensive internal damage. The internal examination disclosed injuries to vital organs and tissues, and the medical officer opined that death occurred on account of shock and haemorrhage resulting from the firearm injuries. PW-2 also examined injured Muhammad Hussain, Haji Sher Afzal and Ghulam Fareed. Thus, the medical evidence establishes not only the homicidal nature of the deaths but also the injuries sustained by the surviving victims during the same occurrence.

12. A distinction must nevertheless be maintained between the evidentiary function of medical testimony and that of ocular evidence. Medical evidence ordinarily establishes the nature, location, probable cause and consequences of injuries; it does not, by itself, establish the identity of the assailant. In “Nasir Ahmed v. The State (2023 SCMR 478)”, the Hon'ble Supreme Court discussed the relationship between medical evidence and an otherwise reliable ocular account. Likewise, in “Muhammad Hanif v. The State (2023 SCMR 2016)”, the Court recognized the sufficiency of trustworthy ocular evidence for sustaining a conviction. In the present case, the medical evidence concerning firearm injuries, the deaths of two persons and the injuries to the survivors are consistent with the occurrence described by the prosecution witnesses. The medical findings are accordingly treated as corroborative, and not as independent proof of the appellant's identity.

13. The prosecution also produced evidence regarding the place of occurrence and the material objects recovered therefrom. PW-3 Fida Rasool acted as a marginal witness to the recovery proceedings. He stated that the investigating officer took into possession bloodstained earth and bloodstained material from different places connected with the injured and deceased persons. He also referred to the collection of twelve empties of 30-bore ammunition and fourteen empties of 7.62-bore ammunition from the place of occurrence through memo Ex.PW-3/1 and Ex.PW-3/2. The appellant was alleged to have been armed with a Kalashnikov, while his co-accused Sher Azam was attributed a pistol. The recovery of empties of both 7.62-bore and 30-bore ammunition is completely compatible with the prosecution version that more than one firearm was used during the occurrence.

14. As regards the alleged delay in registration of the FIR, the record shows that the occurrence took place at about 8:30 p.m. on 25.07.2011 and that the complainant reported the matter at about 9:45 p.m. while in an injured condition. The report was followed by the formal registration of the FIR. The intervening period has to be considered in the context of the number of casualties, the removal of injured persons for medical attention and the distance between the place of occurrence and the police station. The initial report was thus made within a comparatively short interval following the incident. There is no material in the available record establishing that the delay was utilized for consultation or fabrication of the allegation against the appellant. The argument based upon delay, therefore, does not provide a sufficient ground for rejecting the prosecution version.

15. It is not disputed that no crime weapon could be recovered from the possession of the appellant. Ordinarily, recovery of the weapon and its forensic connection with the empties may provide corroboration. Its absence, however, does not invariably defeat a prosecution case which is otherwise established through reliable direct evidence. In Ansar’s case ibid, the Hon'ble Supreme Court considered the evidentiary worth of weapon recoveries alongside otherwise reliable ocular and medical evidence and recognized that an inconsequential recovery does not necessarily absolve an accused whose guilt is proved through independent evidence. In the instant case, the appellant was arrested almost ten years after the occurrence. The absence of weapon recovery is therefore a deficiency in the available corroborative material, but it does not, by itself, invalidate the direct evidence of the eyewitnesses.

16. The record indicates that the appellant remained unavailable to the investigating agency for several years and was apprehended only on 21.03.2021. It must be emphasized that abscondence is not substantive evidence of guilt. A person may remain unavailable to the law-enforcement authorities for reasons which do not necessarily establish his participation in an offence. Nevertheless, where the prosecution has otherwise produced credible evidence connecting an accused with the occurrence, unexplained and prolonged abscondence may be considered as an additional corroborative circumstance. The appellant's absence for approximately ten years, therefore, cannot replace proof of his participation, but may be considered along with the independent prosecution evidence.

17. So far as motive is concerned, the prosecution alleged that a dispute between the children of the parties led to the convening of a Jirga and ultimately to the occurrence. The statements of PW-6 and PW-7 provide direct evidence concerning the Jirga, while the other prosecution witnesses furnish supporting details regarding the circumstances in which the parties came together. The existence of such a dispute provides a background for the incident. Motive, even when established, is ordinarily a supporting circumstance and not a substitute for reliable evidence of the actual commission of the offence. In the present case, the direct evidence regarding the occurrence, is found sufficient to connect the appellant with the commission of the offence, while the motive alleged by the prosecution further supports the gathering of injured and deceased during proceedings of that Jirga.

18. Upon a cumulative appraisal of the material, we find that the prosecution witnesses have provided a substantially consistent account of the occurrence. PW-5 Mst. Nageena Bibi and PW-6 Ghulam Fareed are injured eyewitnesses whose presence receives support from the medical evidence. PW-7 Abdul Malik, a participant in the Jirga, supplies additional evidence regarding the events preceding the firing and the participation of the appellant. The medical testimony of PW-1 and PW-2 establishes the firearm injuries, the resulting deaths and the injuries sustained by the surviving victims. The investigating witnesses and the documentary material further establish the investigation of a firearm occurrence at the relevant place. The evidence thus comprises mutually supporting circumstances rather than isolated or unconnected allegations.

19. A criminal case is not to be decided by an arithmetical comparison of every sentence uttered by each witness. The decisive test is whether a contradiction affects a material fact upon which the prosecution case depends. Variations concerning peripheral details, particularly where witnesses observed different stages of a sudden occurrence, cannot be placed on the same footing as contradictions concerning the identity of the assailant, the location of the occurrence or the essential manner in which the offence was committed. In Ansar’s case (ibid), the Hon'ble Supreme Court reiterated the distinction between minor discrepancies and material contradictions. Applying that test to the evidence before us, the inconsistencies reflected in the available record do not appear to undermine the central allegation of the appellant's participation in the firing. The testimony of the injured eyewitnesses, supported by the medical circumstances and the account of the Jirga participant, supplies direct evidence of the appellant's involvement. No material has been demonstrated which would render that evidence inherently improbable or establish a reasonable basis for concluding that the appellant was substituted for some unidentified actual assailant. In the case of “Muhammad Riaz v. Khurram Shehzad and another (2024 SCMR 51)”, it was emphasized that the credibility of the witnesses, the nature of inconsistencies and the relationship between ocular and medical evidence must all be examined before reaching a finding regarding guilt.

20. In light of the above discussion, we are satisfied that the prosecution has succeeded in establishing the appellant's active participation in the armed occurrence. The ocular account, read with the medical and other evidence, proves that the appellant resorted to firing with a deadly weapon during the Jirga incident, which resulted in the deaths of Muhammad Ilyas and Mst. Robina Bibi and injuries to the other victims. The evidence, considered as a whole, is sufficient to maintain the convictions under section 302(b), PPC, and the other applicable penal provisions. The question of sentence, particularly the capital sentence awarded under section 302(b), PPC, however, requires separate consideration. The gravity of the offence and the number of victims are important, but the Court must also examine whether mitigating circumstances exist which would justify imprisonment for life instead of death. In “Muhammad Yasin and another v. The State and others (2024 SCMR 128)”, the Hon'ble Supreme Court considered the effect of an unproved motive and other mitigating circumstances upon the quantum of punishment under section 302(b), PPC. Similarly, in “Maskeen Ullah and another v. The State and another (2023 SCMR 1568)”, the Court considered the absence of established motive and certain deficiencies in the corroborative evidence while examining the propriety of the capital sentence. These authorities require the Court to address the question of punishment independently of the finding regarding guilt. However, in the instant case, the motive of quarrel between the children followed by convening of a Jirag, stands sufficiently proved.

21. Moreover, in the present case, the prosecution evidence attributes to the appellant a leading and active role in the occurrence. He was allegedly armed with a Kalashnikov and, instead of permitting the dispute to be resolved through the Jirga, resorted to firing upon the persons assembled there. The resulting violence did not remain confined to a single person; it caused the deaths of Muhammad Ilyas and Mst. Robina Bibi and injuries to several others. The evidence does not disclose that the deceased persons were armed or that they had launched any attack upon the appellant. The firing, as described by the eyewitnesses, was directed at persons gathered in connection with the dispute and those who subsequently approached the scene. These circumstances, demonstrate a degree of aggression and disregard for human life which bears materially upon the question of sentence.

22. We are mindful that non-recovery of the weapon and the need to assess the motive independently are relevant considerations when determining whether the capital sentence should be maintained. Nevertheless, the effect of those circumstances cannot be determined mechanically; it must depend upon whether they create uncertainty regarding the nature of the appellant's participation or otherwise constitute mitigating circumstances. In the case before us, the prosecution has produced direct testimony assigning the appellant an active role in the firing, and the fatal consequences of the occurrence are established through medical evidence. The deaths of two persons and injuries to several others are not being relied upon merely for their emotional gravity, but as consequences of the armed assault attributed to the appellant. The non-recovery of the alleged crime weapon was justified due to long abscondence of the appellant. Upon evaluation of the established circumstances, no mitigating feature of sufficient weight emerges from the available record to justify substitution of the capital sentence with imprisonment for life.

23. Before parting with the judgment, it is appropriate to reiterate that the function of an appellate Court in a criminal appeal is not merely to ascertain whether another view of the evidence is possible, but to determine whether the finding of guilt is supported by reliable evidence satisfying the prescribed criminal standard of proof. Where material doubt exists, the accused must receive its benefit; conversely, where the prosecution evidence, fairly and independently examined, establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the conviction cannot be disturbed on the basis of immaterial discrepancies or conjectural possibilities. In the present case, the principal prosecution witnesses have provided a consistent account of the appellant's participation, supported by the medical circumstances, and the defence objections do not create reasonable doubt regarding the essential elements of the offence.

24. For the reasons recorded above, we find that the prosecution has successfully proved its case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. The impugned judgment dated 18.01.2025, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Haripur at Ghazi, insofar as it relates to the convictions and sentences of the appellant, is supported by the evidence and does not warrant interference in appellate jurisdiction. Consequently, the instant criminal appeal is dismissed and the convictions and sentences awarded to the appellant Muhammad Afsar are maintained. The murder reference sent by the learned trial Court stands confirmed.
Announced.
Dt. 27.10.2026 J U D G E J U D G E Tufail/* Hon’ble Justices Abdul Fayaz & Syed Mudasser Ameer.
